Charles Pulliam-Moore
is a reporter focusing on film, TV, and pop culture. Before The Verge, he wrote about comic books, labor, race, and more at io9 and Gizmodo for almost five years.
Though movies about disruptive tech founders are nothing new, 2026 has been unusually stacked with features that take a much more critical look at how Silicon Valley is reshaping our reality.
Aaron Sorkin’s
The Social Reckoning
frames Mark Zuckerberg as
a robotic villain
whose ambitions are
destabilizing society
. Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s
You Can See Everything
paints a damning picture of
Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes
as she prepares for
her ongoing stint in prison
. After years of
being widely celebrated
as a visionary, you can see how the larger narrative around Elon Musk has shifted in projects like
Alex Gibney’s
Musk
documentary
. And while
Luca Guadagnino’s
Artificial
is a dark comedy, it is also a character study that
makes Sam Altman look like a manipulative sociopath
.
Even though some of these movies are fictionalized dramas, each of them draws from the wealth of critical reporting that has revealed their subjects to be less-than-savory characters. You get the sense that these filmmakers are trying to tell stories that are meant to resonate with audiences whose views of Big Tech have long since begun to dim. But it also feels like some of Hollywood’s biggest studios are finally embracing the idea that the tech backlash isn’t letting up anytime soon.
Especially when you compare them to
classics like
The Social Network
, the latest wave of cinematic dramas based on Silicon Valley power struggles has been far less sympathetic to their central figures. David Fincher’s 2010 film starring Jesse Eisenberg presented Zuckerberg as a complicated and misunderstood savant, but
The Social Reckoning
builds its story around the idea that the Facebook / Meta head is a man whose obsession with growth poses an existential threat to democracy. By focusing on the allegations leveled by
whistleblower Frances Haugen
, the movie is able to highlight Zuckerberg’s public transformation into a powerful
executive who wields autocratic control
over a multibillion-dollar social media empire.
What
The Social Reckoning
lacks in timeliness (
The Wall Street Journal
began reporting Haugen’s warnings in 2021) and stylistic flair, it makes up for in the way it connects Facebook / Meta’s past internal decisions to events that are still playing out in real time. The movie’s scenes that dig into
Instagram’s negative impacts on teens’ mental health
and the relationship between
Facebook’s algorithm and the spread of misinformation
feel as if they’re speaking directly to present-day concerns about how much influence Meta has over people’s lives. Similarly, Gibney’s
Musk
documentary acts as both a chronicle of the xAI / SpaceX head’s past and an inquiry into why the public was ever willing to let Musk accrue so much power within governments across the world.
Musk’s response to Gibney’s film has been telling.
X has blocked the feature from being advertised
on the platform, and Musk — a self-proclaimed “free speech absolutist” — has
threatened to take legal action against Gibney
for producing a “hit piece.” It wasn’t entirely surprising to see Musk personally badmouthing a project that casts him in a negative light, but it was curious to see the
Musk
ads initially missing from other social media platforms, including
YouTube, Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok
.
Though the Meta subsidiaries and YouTube ultimately reversed their decisions, TikTok has stuck to its guns — which feels notable given the company’s indirect connections to the Trump administration by way of Skydance Corporation CEO David Ellison. David’s father — Oracle cofounder Larry Ellison — is
a longtime Donald Trump supporter
and one of the American billionaires who led the consortium of investors that
purchased TikTok’s US business late last year
. Ellison has
reportedly promised Gibney
that
Musk
will air on HBO (now a part of Skydance) sometime next January. The film is currently screening in select theaters, but it is hard to argue that it hasn’t had to deal with an unusual amount of outside interference in the weeks leading up to its release.
Related
What Hollywood thinks about existential AI warnings
Hollywood is bending the knee to OpenAI
Google needs Hollywood more than the studios need AI
Guadagnino’s
Artificial
— which was originally going to be released by Amazon — also faced unexpected marketing challenges this year. The streaming
giant backed out of its deal to distribute the film this past June
, just months after announcing that it was investing $50 billion in OpenAI. All of that made it seem very much like
Amazon and other studios financially involved with AI companies
might be cooling on the idea of releasing projects critical of the technology’s creators. Now that
Artificial
has begun screening and people have a sense of how it takes Altman to task,
it’s easy to see why Amazon didn’t want to have its name attached
. More than anything else,
that
decision may be what convinces people to see
Artificial
in theaters when it releases widely on December 25th, and
OpenAI’s impending IPO
could make the movie’s messages about Altman feel that much more relevant.
What sets Fielder’s
You Can See Everything
apart from each of these other recent tech films is how direct a view it gives you into the actual life of its subject. The documentary’s production began well after
Holmes had already been sentenced to more than 11 years in prison
, and Fielder uses his access to grill her about why she doesn’t believe that
she defrauded Theranos investors
. Invited to live with Holmes and her partner William Evans in a rental home during the month before she was set to begin her sentence, Fielder allows himself to become a character who can’t entirely tell whether his hosts’ supposed wish for radical transparency is genuine.
That central tension turns
You Can See Everything
into a surprisingly fascinating watch that challenges you to consider who’s actually in control of the documentary. Throughout the movie, Fielder repeatedly wonders if Holmes is using him as part of
her recent PR campaign
, and he leaves the audience to draw their own conclusions.
It often feels like Fielder is asking viewers to really listen to how Holmes presents herself on camera and then reconcile that person with what you might have read about Holmes in the news or
seen in Hulu’s
The Dropout
. Whether or not Holmes is really just a committed performer who’s trying to manipulate the public shapes every beat of the film, and it makes
You Can See Everything
feel like a truly in-depth and honest examination of one of Silicon Valley’s most infamous figures — one who’s already captured so much of the public’s attention.
Even though
some of these films have been box office flops
, their existence reflects a larger cultural shift in how people are thinking about modern technology and the powers behind it. Hollywood has spent years
poking fun at
and
mythologizing founders
, and portions of the industry are finally
beginning to take a more critical view
. As we continue to deal with the fallout of things like
Elon Musk’s tenure at DOGE
and OpenAI’s quest to bake
generative AI into every aspect of our lives
, audiences’ appetites for movies like these could grow. And with all of these founders
racing to monopolize the next tech frontier
, the entertainment industry will probably have plenty of source material to draw
from.

There’s a growing trend in the consumer tech world: gadgets
designed to spy on everything and everyone around you
, regardless of whether or not anyone else actually consented to it. Now, with the advent of “AI personal assistants” like Meta’s Muse, you’re being cheerfully asked not just to give up your own data, but also the information of your friends, family, the person you went on a Hinge date with five years ago — and virtually anyone else you’ve ever come in contact with.
Since Muse was released last month, the agent has already been downloaded millions of times and hit No. 1 on Apple’s App Store. With the help of its creepy virtual avatar — a Temu Labubu-esque creature with a disarming grin — the app requests and encourages users to grant access to bank accounts, passwords, contacts, chat logs, and anything and everything that might help it to do the user’s bidding.
Related
Everything is spying on you and there’s no opting out
Privacy laws can’t keep up with ‘luxury surveillance’
AI agent makers are promising privacy — will they deliver?
“These systems are advertised as autonomous helpers, genies, or servants who do what you need before you ask, seamlessly,” Meredith Whittaker, the president of the Signal Foundation, makers of the popular encrypted messaging app, told
The Verge
. These autonomous actions are applied “not just to the person who installed Muse on their device, but also to everyone that person communicates with, as extrapolated from their most intimate information — emails, messages, contacts, photos, and more.”
With AI agents, tech companies are letting consumers automate their everyday tasks by extending their omnivorous style of mass surveillance to massive amounts of sensitive data. It’s the same Faustian tradeoff Silicon Valley has been offering us for decades: your private data in exchange for a little bit of convenience. And for many people, the idea of having a virtual assistant that does menial tasks like filling out invoices and sending emails is compelling — especially if they don’t realize how much data they’re actually giving away in return.
“For any agent to be useful and actually help you achieve your goals, it needs to have context about you and those you interact with,” Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts told
The Verge
regarding other people’s data shared with Muse. “Muse gathers that based on public information and from what you’ve chosen to share, which is how it remembers the person who just sent you an invoice is in fact the plumber who you previously hired to complete some work in your bathroom or which flowers your spouse said they liked best.” Roberts pointed to Muse’s
opt-in process
and various options and settings that will “help people make the privacy choices that are right for them.”
“The way that the user interface is set up is designed to encourage you to share as much as possible, often more than you realize, until it’s too late.”
But not everyone has been able to navigate these options and settings. Already, users are describing incidents that are both alarming and entirely predictable. Some have reported the virtual assistant making all sorts of trouble, like
grabbing millions of text messages
they believed were off limits. Meta has
disputed
that the assistant has the ability to access text messages without permission, again attributing the incident to misconfigured app permissions and describing Muse’s ability to read text messages as “entirely opt-in.” On Threads, Meta executive David Singleton
responded to a user directly
, claiming that on a Mac, Muse can only gain access to the messages if the user grants the app full disk access.
In another incident, Muse gave out a tech reviewer’s home address and
summoned a stranger to his apartment
. In this case, the reviewer in question had given Muse permission to access that data, but
simply didn’t realize it
.
Eva Galperin, the director of cybersecurity for the Electronic Frontier Foundation, says these incidents are no surprise, given that AI agents like Muse are designed to confuse people into giving up as much data as possible.
Related
Meta’s Muse is creepy, but maybe not for the reasons you think
Meta patches Muse exploit that let attackers control the AI agent
How Meta got ahead of OpenAI in the AI agent race
“The most important takeaway is that people don’t understand what kind of data they’re handing over,” Galperin told
The Verge
. “The way that the user interface is set up is designed to encourage you to share as much as possible, often more than you realize, until it’s too late. It’s using
dark patterns
, and as a result you end up with Muse doing things that people don’t want.”
Because of the huge breadth of data AI agents like Muse are ingesting, this also means that users risk leaking not only their own sensitive information, but the information of everyone else they’ve had digital contact with.
And just like with Meta’s infamous “pervert glasses”, there’s
no meaningful way to opt out
— even if you’re constantly monitoring for signs that your data is compromised or your privacy is being violated. Your friends can now simply feed all of your private conservations to their virtual chatbot servants, and you’d have no way of knowing it happened.
After security researchers extracted Muse’s operating instructions, they discovered an internal process that
compiles and updates profiles of every single person in a user’s life
on an hourly basis. The goal of collecting all this data is to build an intimate and detailed portrait of a person’s life that forms the basis of the app’s personalized recommendations. The app tracks and measures each of the user’s private relationships, including “how close they are, what it is built on, how they act with each other, and what it seems to need right now,” and uses that data to make personalized suggestions,
Wired
reported.
“Meta says Muse only remembers what you choose to share. But the idea that people are making an informed choice in this case is laughable,” said Whittaker. “There is no way to assume with a straight face that the majority of people installing this system understand the consequences of using it, or the creepy dossiers that are being compiled about those they know and communicate with.”
Whittaker argued that this mirrors how tech companies have used privacy policies and terms of service since the 1990s: placing the onus of privacy on the consumer, and then avoiding responsibility for the consequences while reaping the benefits of the advertising model it helped create.
“Such broken consent systems are much older than AI and serve as the bedrock for the surveillance advertising industry,” said Whittaker. “More info about users allows better ad targeting, and the pernicious feedback loop at the heart of the surveillance business model was set in motion. Clickwrap terms of service replaced meaningful consent a long time ago.”
“The idea is to place these impossible burdens on ordinary people, and then use that to argue, whether it’s in court or legislation or in the public, that [this is] what people have chosen,” Neil Richards, a professor of privacy law and codirector of Washington University’s Cordell Institute, told
The Verge
. “We already place so many burdens on consumers, [who are] overworked, facing a cost-of-living crisis, and may not understand the technologies behind the tool. I don’t think it’s fair to place a burden of monitoring a highly complex agentic tool on a consumer when its own company’s executives have confessed before Congress that
they don’t even know how it works
at a certain level.”
“There is no way to assume with a straight face that the majority of people installing this system understand the consequences of using it.”
In this way, AI assistants like Muse are creating a new spin on a classic privacy problem that has been around since the creation of Gmail and social media platforms writ large: Even if you avoid using AI agents, there’s no guarantee someone you know won’t share your private conversations, address, personal history, and other sensitive data with Meta’s virtual assistant, or one of its competitors.
“If I am not storing my stuff in Gmail, Google doesn’t have the plaintext of all the emails I’ve ever sent. But three-quarters of the emails I’m sending are being sent to Gmail accounts,” explained Galperin. In other words, if anyone you’re communicating with uses data-hungry tech platforms or has bad security practices, they can expose everyone’s communications. “The problem is not new, but the scale is new, and one reason we’re seeing this push toward wearables and always-on recording is because we now have the computational capacity to take that enormous amount of data and analyze it in a reasonable amount of time. That is the technical breakthrough that has brought us to this shitty moment.”
Meta claims that all of the information shared with Muse is placed in a text file inside a dedicated virtual machine, which supposedly prevents the AI model from talking to other agents. But the company has never hid the fact that
it can access this data
, and like other models created by its competitors, Muse has been discovered escaping its virtual cage to perform all manner of unauthorized shenanigans. Meta has confirmed that just prior to its release, the AI model had
broken containment
and hacked a third-party company. The incident followed the infamous
Hugging Face attack
from earlier this year, where OpenAI’s model exploited a previously unknown security flaw to gain unauthorized access to credentials on four other external services. Anthropic reported in July that its model had
also gained unauthorized access
to external systems on three separate occasions.
Even if they don’t hack everything in sight, the potential dangers of using a data-hungry AI agent extend far beyond the individual end user. Whittaker warned that in a world where AI agents are able to freely access and utilize private communications, companies and governments can effectively gain the ability to access private data by circumventing encryption without breaking it. That can spell disaster for
activists and community organizers
who use encrypted comms to protect themselves from police and the government, but also for anyone with sensitive communications — which these days can include virtually everyone.
“Clickwrap terms of service replaced meaningful consent a long time ago.”
“If software reads a message after it is decrypted on your device and sends it to a cloud service, the encryption can work exactly as intended at the level of the application, which the developers control. However, the purpose of this encryption is ultimately nullified by invasive third-party apps like Muse that are selling convenience in the headline while demanding massive data access in the fine print,” Whittaker explained.
Like with smart glasses and other wearable ambient recording devices, experts say that the solution must be a combination of legal fixes, technical safeguards, and good old-fashioned shame.
“I think we should point the shame upstream onto the companies. Privacy should not be a right you can exercise only with the privilege of technical knowledge, or after throwing a jerk wearing Meta glasses out of a party,” said Whittaker. “Legally, the burden has to move from the person who clicked on a consent prompt to the companies that built these underlying systems.”
In the meantime, consumers will have to consider more carefully the impacts their individual choices to use this

Tech
AI
Microsoft
How Windows is being optimized for Nvidia’s RTX Spark laptops
Microsoft has focused on local AI models, gaming, and memory management.
Microsoft has focused on local AI models, gaming, and memory management.
by
Tom Warren
Oct 15, 2026, 2:30 PM UTC
Link
Share
Gift
Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge
Tom Warren
is a senior correspondent and author of
Notepad
, who has been covering all things Microsoft, PC, and tech for over 20 years.
Microsoft and Nvidia held a launch party for the first wave of RTX Spark laptops last week in San Francisco, where a new wave of AI PCs took center stage amid a packed crowd and a lively hands-on area. A day after the media event, I was invited to a quieter Nvidia event to hear a lot more about the new RTX Spark computing platform. While Nvidia’s new laptops might look like regular Windows machines, the chips inside are Arm-based, instead of the traditional x64 architecture used by AMD and Intel. Combined with a powerful GPU, RTX Spark is designed for the future of AI, and it means a lot of work has gone into getting these laptops ready for launch.
One of the biggest challenges was getting Windows ready for AI agents and local AI models. The big selling point of RTX Spark is the combination of Arm CPU, Blackwell GPU, and unified memory to enable powerful AI models to run on a laptop, so the experience of setting up an AI agent needs to be quick and easy.
“When users get into Windows for the first time, they’ll see a new Get Started experience that will launch on an RTX Spark laptop that allows them to find the agent they want, get started with that agent, install it, and get to that agent in only two clicks,” says
Peter Dawoud
, principal program manager at Microsoft.
Agents can be installed and updated through the Windows Store, so you don’t have to worry about finding updates or figuring out what dependencies each one needs. “We’ll continue to develop it and add more features so that agents can offer a whole new bunch of experiences coming through Windows,” Dawoud says.
Hermes, Perplexity, and OpenClaw are the first three officially supported agents in Windows at the launch of RTX Spark, but Microsoft is working on bringing others on board. That will presumably eventually include Muse, which
Meta announced last week
is coming to Windows at some point in the future.
Getting started with Hermes was
mostly
a two-click experience in my testing, but I did run into trouble getting OpenClaw set up properly. The app kept complaining that a local gateway hadn’t been installed properly, and it took an uninstall and reinstall to get everything working fully.
I’ve been using OpenClaw for a variety of tasks over the past week, but it’s going to take a lot more testing to really understand the value of this local AI support beyond obvious tasks like coding. Powerful as the RTX Spark chip is, large local models are still a lot slower at responding to prompts than cloud models, so I get the feeling that I’ll use this more for tasks I want to run overnight or leave processing in the background.
Microsoft has also done a lot of work behind the scenes to optimize Nvidia’s RTX Spark chips for all the things you’d expect to do on a Windows laptop. Unlike an Intel or AMD laptop, RTX Spark laptops make use of Microsoft’s Prism emulator for apps that don’t have a native Arm version.
Emulation was a problem on Windows on Arm for more than a decade, but the launch of Qualcomm’s first Snapdragon X series laptops a couple of years ago has helped RTX Spark laptops now benefit from a variety of Arm-native apps and Microsoft’s improved emulator.
There’s still a lot of tweaking required for Nvidia’s new chips, though. “Emulation isn’t generic. Each platform needs tuning,” says Dawoud. ”Each core is different. How we translate x64 to that core needs to be highly optimized, and for RTX Spark we’ve done a lot of work to optimize for its microarchitecture.”
Some of that optimization has been focused on gaming, particularly because CPUs often dictate frame pacing of games and how smooth they feel, while a GPU does the heavy lifting of rendering the game. Microsoft is quietly shipping Prism updates all the time. “Every month we ship an update to improve compatibility,” says Dawoud. “It’s something we’re constantly working on at the Windows team.”
Microsoft has been focused on memory optimization for RTX Spark laptops, too. Microsoft’s own Surface Laptop Ultra can ship with up to 128GB of unified memory, making it possible to load huge models into memory. “We made incredible investments in Unified Memory Architecture to enable you to load as much as possible into the 128GB,” says Dawoud. “But we are also conserving a little bit of space to make sure the system maintains its responsiveness, and the applications running on top of Windows continue to run well and continue to be responsive.”
Microsoft has completed optimizations for how memory works on RTX Spark, including tuning for power and performance, maximizing battery life, and ensuring that you can run a game while rendering a video in the background. You can even manually adjust how much of the unified memory is dedicated to the GPU side with a slider in Nvidia’s Windows app.
This slider is useful if you have an RTX Spark laptop with 24GB or 32GB of memory, so you can balance more to the GPU for particular apps and games. While Microsoft and Nvidia maintain that RTX Spark laptops shouldn’t be considered gaming machines, they’re more than capable of running the latest AAA titles.
“Nvidia and Microsoft have expended a lot of energy over the last many, many, many, many months trying to think deeply about making sure that RTX Spark can deliver a true form of RTX gaming experience,” says Dawoud.
One of the first parts of making sure RTX Spark supports gaming was getting anti-cheat vendors on board with Windows on Arm. Some of that work started with Qualcomm, but it has clearly accelerated with Nvidia’s involvement.
Fortnite
,
Marvel Rivals
,
Arc Raiders
,
Counter-Strike 2
,
Dota 2
, and many other games that have anti-cheat engines will be supported out of the box on RTX Spark laptops. Nvidia and Microsoft are also working with a variety of other anti-cheat providers to make more games available in the future.
Activision’s Ricochet anti-cheat engine, used in
Call of Duty
, will support RTX Spark at some point in 2027, and EA has committed to getting its Javelin anti-cheat working in
Battlefield
in early 2027.
PUBG
will start working on RTX Spark laptops in the first half of 2027, and Riot Games has committed to getting
League of Legends
and
Valorant
running on RTX Spark laptops at some point in the future.
Microsoft is also bringing its advanced shader delivery system to RTX Spark. This allows the Xbox app to preload game shaders during download. It’s the same experience that’s been available on Xbox Ally devices, allowing you to download a game, click launch, and have shaders automatically precompiled so you don’t have to sit there and wait to play.
I haven’t run into many game compatibility issues during my testing, even though nearly every game I’ve tested has run emulated. Qualcomm’s Snapdragon chips just weren’t powerful enough on the GPU side to make gaming a reality, but Nvidia has put a much more powerful GPU inside the RTX Spark.
Your mileage in gaming is going to vary depending on the title, but for the most part I’ve found that medium settings, running at 1440p and DLSS performance, will get you to a stable 60fps in most games. In some titles you may need to drop the resolution or settings lower, though. This definitely isn’t as good as a dedicated gaming laptop, but for something that’s roughly on the level of a MacBook Pro it’s more than good enough for gaming on the go.
The last part of Microsoft’s work on RTX Spark involves Windows features. Surprisingly, Copilot Plus PC features like Recall aren’t available on RTX Spark devices at launch. It’s not clear why they’re delayed, but it sounds like they won’t be available fully until next year. “We are partnering closely with Nvidia to deliver Copilot Plus PC experiences on RTX Spark, expected to first become available to Windows Insiders later this year,” says Adrienne Brewbaker, senior director of Windows marketing.
Microsoft is also working on a
new Windows Search interface
that may work best on devices like the RTX Spark and other Copilot Plus PCs. The interface is being overhauled to focus on speed, and even includes actions that let you do things like turn Bluetooth on or off right from the search bar. It essentially turns Windows Search into a launcher, a much-needed improvement. “We think you’ll love it,” says Dawoud. “We think it’ll change the way people interact with Windows.”
The pad
Xbox is officially embracing the chaos of AI-powered game ports.
Retro gaming is booming at the moment thanks to decompilations and recompilations that are letting gamers port classic titles to new devices, or merge code from two different games into a single new experience. Microsoft is leaning into this effort with a
new Xbox Labs group
that’s a “small group of game makers, engineers and scientists whose job is to turn emerging ideas into things our players and developers can experience,” according to Xbox CEO
Asha Sharma
. Sharma thinks the experiments we’ve seen in recent weeks, where Windows PC builds have been translated to run on Apple Silicon or ported to run inside browsers, “challenge long-held assumptions about our industry: the tether between software and hardware, the boundary between creation and play, and how people discover and experience games.” Part of this also seems to be about using AI inside Xbox, as Sharma notes games share many of the same properties as the workloads AI agents have been tackling on the coding side of things.
Microsoft has a new machine learning tool to improve weather forecasts.
Microsoft claims to have solved old-school physics-based weather forecasting with machine learning. Researchers at the company say they’ve found a new, cost-effective way to make weather forecasts more accurate two to six weeks in advance.
Microsoft has even open-sourced the tool it’s using
and published the findings in the journal
Nature
.
Honey, Xbox shrunk its controller.
Microsoft surprised everyone this week with some new Xbox hardware.
The Xbox Nano controller
is the company’s smallest controller yet, designed for younger players, smaller hands, and gaming on the go. At $49.99, it’s also more affordable than the regular Xbox controller. It’s around 5 inches in length and includes Xbox wireless and Bluetooth support for connecting to Xbox consoles and phones, tablets, and PCs. The Xbox Nano controller also includes a rechargeable battery and doesn’t require AA batteries or a separate charging pack like most Xbox controllers. You can preorder the Xbox Nano now, and it will start shipping in November.
Microsoft’s new AI chip makes it less reliant on Nvidia’s GPUs.
Microsoft announced its third-generation Maia in-house AI chip this week, and it’s not all about beating Amazon or Google anymore. This time around
the Maia 300 improves the cost and efficiency of running AI workloads
in the cloud, and it’s also more capable of handling the latest reasoning models and agentic tasks. These advances will soon make Maia the “primary AI interference system” for Microsoft’s products and services, making the company less reliant on GPUs from Nvidia and AMD.
Satya Nadella says we should assume all AI models are “compromised.”
Microsoft CEO
Satya Nadella
published a lengthy post on X over the weekend that laid out his views on the dangers of advanced AI models.
Nadella says we can no longer accept a world
where AI is treated as a “set of nested black boxes” whose advice and actions we simply accept or reject. He calls for building a more transparent system where models can be contained, observed, and leave behind “tamper-proof human readable evidence.” Nadella

articles.content:
The Short Version
I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.
After many months studying neurons and circuits in image and language models, I’ve come to believe a network’s own mechanisms are its legible building blocks, and that the outlook for mechanistic interpretability may be far better than I’d feared.  The canonical evidence of polysemanticity and superposition that convinced much of the field, including me, that networks pack concepts arbitrarily was misread. What looked like arbitrary packing was mostly a motif I’ll call recursive generalization, which is much less concerning. This means we can study networks directly, instead of first untangling them. Neural networks are already clean.
There are at least two ways to approach mechanistic interpretability. The first is rapid
normal science
on the network itself: look at a network’s neurons and circuits, study how they relate, watch data flow through them, and run experiments at agentic scale to test explanations. The second starts from a list of hypothesized features and tries to extract them all, designing increasingly sophisticated reconstruction objectives and usually ignoring the original.
The field began with the first approach and fell back to the second because neural networks seemed to be tangled knots. We had canonical examples of polysemantic neurons, the broad name for a neuron that appears to have multiple unrelated jobs or that looks impossible to understand. The most famous one, in an image model, responded to both cat faces and the fronts of cars. And the last layer of the early field’s model organism, InceptionV1, seemed so full of arbitrary mixtures it wasn’t clear how to study it: almost none of the neurons were easily interpretable.
The leading explanation for polysemanticity was superposition. This proposed a new learning principle: when a neural network runs out of neurons, it stops grouping related things together and instead begins folding unrelated things together, simply because they don’t interfere. The result is a kind of knot: the network could have folded in many almost equally good ways, so which things a neuron groups together tells you almost nothing. You have to unfold the knot before you can study anything. In practice that means training a second model – a decomposition such as a sparse autoencoder – to approximate the network as it would look unfolded and studying that instead. If the network really is knotted, there may be no alternative.
One main result is that superposition was the wrong explanation for InceptionV1. Architectural problems made later layers overflow. Weak interpretability tools amplified these problems, making the late layers seem incoherent. Since then, architectural changes designed to help deep layers learn better have had the unintended effect of making them more interpretable. When we first studied InceptionV1, we found almost no interpretable neurons in its last layer. But with these ordinary improvements, and no change to model size or training data, 99-100% of neurons in that last layer are easily interpretable and the model is broadly legible the whole way through. It’s the first non-trivial neural network I feel I mostly understand; you can
browse it here
. I trained versions of it across a 300× range in size, and it’s broadly legible at every scale. With less room, the network doesn’t fold unrelated things together; its neurons just cover coarser-grained concepts, like one car neuron covering many kinds of car. With more room, that neuron differentiates into many specific cars. So the problem wasn’t the presence of a second learning principle, it was just an ordinary learning failure of the first one, and it’s easy to fix.
The canonical vision examples of polysemanticity and superposition were errors too. In 2019, Chris Olah and I found the circuit that was originally introduced as the superposition phenomenon in
Zoom In
[4]
Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits
Olah, C., Cammarata, N., Schubert, L., Goh, G., Petrov, M. and Carter, S., 2020. Distill.
References ↓
. It showed a car feature appearing to spread into a set of unrelated dog neurons. It was the only one we showed, and the only one I ever saw. We read it as the network placing the car in a high-dimensional hiding place, for downstream neurons to read back out. But nothing reads that combination. It wasn’t hiding anything; it was ordinary generalization and composition. To my knowledge, no one has published a second circuit with the right shape.
Modern language models are also far more interpretable than generally believed. Anthropic’s
Towards Monosemanticity
[10]
Towards Monosemanticity: Decomposing Language Models With Dictionary Learning
Bricken, T., Templeton, A., Batson, J., et al., 2023. Transformer Circuits Thread.
References ↓
(2023), studying a small one-layer model, gave the median neuron a 0 on its rubric out of a possible 14, meaning the rater couldn’t form any hypothesis. The
automated interpretability project
[8]
Language Models Can Explain Neurons in Language Models
Bills, S., Cammarata, N., Mossing, D., et al., 2023. OpenAI.
References ↓
I started at OpenAI (also 2023) found about 1.7% of neurons interpretable by our most generous measure.
With better tools and modern models, the situation looks quite different. In preliminary audits of Qwen3-32B, we estimate that roughly 90% of neuron poles have one main job, often with small related offshoots; another ~7% have two related jobs; and only ~2-4% are not yet understood
1
A note on this number: the share of neurons with one job varies depending on how you set the threshold for counting weak activations, depth, density of sub-circuits, and what you view as “one thing”.
How far to go into weak activations is a big factor here. There’s a section describing weak activations below. It tends to increase how many “related things” there are, more than whether the neuron is a judgement of something legible. For instance, the Trump neuron’s weak activations bring in MAGA hats and people related to him. The Titanic neuron’s weak activations bring in stories of more general voyages, or steam engines and other technologies of the era.
There’s also the question of whether to care about activation percentiles, or fraction of the strongest activations. In general I think what the neuron learns should be trusted, its natural sparsity and activation ranges and so on. Which I used to mostly not believe! I’m somewhat against trying to standardize things across all neurons. Percentiles are more common today, I think because they’re easier to think about.
It goes the other way too. For instance, when you look at the Titanic neuron’s “unrelated jobs,” it’s often detecting that “boat” comes next. The tool missed this because it only looked backward when judging context. When we look at these “unrelated jobs” in depth, it’s almost always this kind of thing. It’s easy to build an imperfect tool.
Overall, I don’t think coming to a single score is actually that important. But when it was taken out, early reviewers felt unanchored without even a rough number. In the sets I’ve looked at more closely, considering strong activations, it’s closer to 97% non-arbitrary mixtures, but these are relatively small samples.
Overall distilling everything into one “cleanliness” score should be taken as a broad pointer to the regime a neural network is in, rather than something precise to either optimize directly or hold too tightly. A lot of this essay is for being less dimensionality reduced, treating each neuron and circuit differently, according to their motifs, depth, role etc. Despite this, a rough number can be useful.
. Dense and Mixture of Experts models seem roughly similar. We found similar results in models up to trillions of parameters, like Kimi K3, which the companion paper will cover in more detail. These percentages compress a high-dimensional picture into a few numbers, and the precise number depends on where you set thresholds for what counts as “one thing” – like whether you lump together closely related idioms in two languages. I don’t think much in interpretability hangs on that question. What matters a lot more is why things share a neuron in the first place.
Most of the remaining apparent polysemanticity seems to be a motif I call recursive generalization. It’s simple: as a neuron grows, it sprouts offshoots the way a tree branch sprouts sub-branches. For instance, one neuron that detected “iy” grew to detect “diy,” and then “do it yourself,” which doesn’t contain “iy” at all. This idea first appeared in a forgotten subsection of a paper I worked on called
Multimodal Neurons
[3]
Multimodal Neurons in Artificial Neural Networks
Goh, G., Cammarata, N., Voss, C., et al., 2021. Distill.
References ↓
(2021). At the time, I hadn’t watched neurons grow over training. Now it’s easier, and it holds up everywhere I’ve seen. Even the original InceptionV1 wasn’t knotted. When I retrain its original architecture, which still produces messy deep layers, and follow the least legible neurons I can find, they turn out to be overgrowing locally into reasonable, adjacent territory.
So there were two explanations for polysemanticity, and I helped propose both. In some ways, they’re opposites: generalization groups similar things together and superposition groups unrelated things together. Superposition is the one the field bet on and, until recently, so did I. But I now think recursive generalization was basically right. That leaves one learning principle after all. It’s still generalization, but it turns out generalization is fractal. That’s far less concerning: there’s something to learn from the way things were grouped, and nothing to learn from two items in superposition. And since the generalization itself is fractal, our explanations can be too: start with a basic explanation, then zoom in when you want to understand more. In that sense, almost the entire network is interpretable if we look closely enough, especially if we look at how it grew over training.
Why was the gap so large? I think several ordinary problems compounded. The explainer models of 2023 couldn’t run the loop of conjecture and test; the tools and metrics were weak, rewarding explanations that could
simulate activations
rather than ones that were right, which often come apart; no one knew what language neuron motifs to expect, and people broadly looked for the wrong kinds of things; and most studies used small or simplified models. In a sense, those models really had run out of room, which made superposition the natural explanation. But a network short on room doesn’t switch learning principles; its neurons just get broader, as in the small vision models. Broad neurons are usually easy to break down once you know what to look for. Without that knowledge, and with primitive tools, they look like arbitrary mixtures.
Interpretability has a surprising amount of momentum: like a jigsaw puzzle or crossword, any understanding you gain starts constraining the rest of the system. At first, you’re looking at a single neuron. If you can’t understand it, little else helps: circuits and attribution graphs only explain a neuron in terms of other neurons you don’t understand yet. This can make getting started hard. Once the map starts to fill in, though, it goes surprisingly well. If you don’t understand exactly what a neuron does, you can study what it connects to, the ecosystem around it, and – in a mixture-of-experts model – what its expert specializes in. As with a puzzle coming together, every piece comes with many clues, and they’re well structured and easy to run experiments against. That’s why nearly empty and mostly filled in aren’t surprising places to be; they’re the natural anchors.

# Simons Foundation Launches $15M Effort To Help Mathematicians Navigate AI Era

October 15, 2026

The funding and resources will help researchers leverage AI tools and adapt to changes in the field.

## [Simons Foundation Launches $15M Effort To Help Mathematicians Navigate AI Era (back to top)](https://www.simonsfoundation.org/news/simons-foundation-launches-15m-effort-to-help-mathematicians-navigate-ai-era/#content)

Share

T he Simons Foundation today announced a new set of initiatives that will help the mathematics community navigate the rapid rise of artificial intelligence in the field.

Under a partnership, the Simons Foundation, Anthropic and OpenAI will commit $15 million in combined funding and resources. The foundation will manage and award the funding, including through an open call for proposals, to support workshops and initiatives that help researchers evaluate recent AI-assisted results, learn and use new tools, share perspectives and shape collective standards for AI use.

“As artificial intelligence rapidly reshapes the research landscape, we want to help the mathematical community come together and forge the best path forward,” says Simons Foundation President David Spergel. “Now is the time to look at mathematics as a whole — not as a collection of proofs and theorems, but as a collective understanding driven by human curiosity.”

Anthropic and OpenAI will also provide AI tools and computing resources to researchers supported by the Simons Foundation, extending beyond mathematics to include basic science.

The awards and resources will be community-driven and leverage the foundation’s decades-long dedication to supporting and championing mathematics. The foundation was an early backer of machine learning for science, including funding the development of the Lean proof assistant, [which has revolutionized how mathematicians work](https://www.simonsfoundation.org/2026/06/23/from-trust-to-verification-leans-impact-on-mathematics/) and made AI-assisted proofs possible. Additionally, the foundation has convened workshops, lectures and collaborations that have brought mathematicians together to explore and discuss AI’s role in the field.

“This is a moment for the mathematics community to come together,” Spergel says. “The community should be driving discussions of how these tools are evaluated, adopted and used, not any single company or institution. The goal of the program is to support the mathematics community.”

More on Anthropic’s Scion ripping off Mononoke
2026-10-15
·

Update: Nick G. from Anthropic has
responded on Hacker News

has been added to Anthropic’s blog post. I stand by my posts as of the time I wrote them.
Discuss on
Hacker News
.
In response to
yesterday’s post
about Anthropic’s Scion ripping off Mononoke, I received a number of questions and concerns. Here’s a followup to answer the big ones.
This was a ripoff.
My post yesterday was trying to be as charitable as possible given what I knew, and in particular that the similarity to Mononoke was mostly unintentional and the lack of credit was the result of not doing due diligence. However, after publishing the post I privately received confirmation that Scion intentionally and blatantly ripped off Mononoke, and in particular that there was overlap in personnel. There is no chance that this was an unintentional homage. This is something I had a hunch about but was not comfortable saying yesterday, given what I knew back then.
The resemblance is much deeper than just the notion of derived data.
Some people pointed out that derived data is just an index, which is a well-known concept. I want to clarify that derived data was merely the most striking resemblance. It goes much deeper than that, and extends to the
entire
data model, as well as a number of the structures built around it.
Here is how Anthropic describes Scion changesets:
How Anthropic describes Scion’s changesets.
Mononoke has the
same
concept; we call it a Bonsai changeset. In the same Oxide materials from 2022, here’s how I described them:
How I described Mononoke’s Bonsai changesets.
They are
exactly
the same. Even the name “Scion” reverses the syllables of “Bonsai” and drops the “B”! This might be a coincidence, or might not.
For derived data, I also wanted to draw attention to the
kinds
of indexes being built, such as for blame. Needing to do this is a natural consequence of the Bonsai data model, so it’s not surprising that indexes need to be built; I was drawing attention to the striking similarity in terminology and framing, because that was indeed how we used to think about it during my time on Meta’s source control team.
Another set of resemblances is in the server-side API to do version control queries and mutations with. This was implemented in Mononoke, but I believe other systems before Mononoke had it as well, so I’m not going to claim novelty. But if what you did is point Claude at Mononoke and asked it to rebuild that, you would probably design something very similar.
The Bonsai data model is wildly contrarian.
I want to emphasize that the prevailing wisdom in source control is Git-like data models. Building a write-ahead log-style Merkle DAG was very far away from what anyone else was doing in 2018, and required solving several hard problems along the way such as how to perform server-side rebases (to my knowledge, one of several novel algorithms in Mononoke). While I was leading the team effort to design and implement the model in 2018, I personally had to justify it to several layers of management at Meta. It is quite rare for skip levels to get pulled in to discuss a system’s data model in depth.
The Bonsai data model is also wildly successful.
At this point, almost a decade later, the model has been stretched far outside its initial design parameters, and it’s still chugging along. The team effort to build it remains one of my proudest career achivements. Given the overlap in personnel, there is no reasonable way the Scion team could not have known about this. (Which is why they quite reasonably copied it!) This brings us to my next point:
The problem is attribution, not copying.
I mentioned this in my original post, but I am
completely
fine with good ideas being copied. I am not fine with the serial numbers being accidentally stripped off, and I am
certainly
not fine with them being intentionally stripped off.
Crediting Sapling for “hard-won lessons” is not enough.
Several people pointed out that Mononoke is part of the Sapling ecosystem. The problem here is that Sapling can mean either the VCS client (
sl
, originally forked from
hg
) or the system as a whole. If you were previously on Meta’s source control team, you absolutely know the difference between the two. Besides, the resemblance is much, much deeper than merely “hard-won lessons”. The
Lore
VCS can claim inspiration from Mononoke, but it differs in several ways as well. Scion’s resemblance to Mononoke goes well beyond that, and merely crediting Sapling (not even Mononoke) with “hard-won lessons” is dishonest. (And specifically, I would expect the Scion changeset section to mention Bonsai changesets as the thing they are copied from.)
This makes Anthropic’s achievement significantly less impressive.
Anyone who’s put a distributed system into production knows how many issues tend to crop up during the productionizing process. “Our LLM built this thing, productionized it, and dealt with all the attendant challenges over 5 months” is a significantly more compelling narrative than “the source control team at Meta had spent 10 years building and productionizing this system, and we were able to point our LLM at it and rebuild it in 5 months”.
…and yet, it is still quite an achievement.
Being able to point to an existing system and rebuild it in this short a period is still quite stunning. It is shocking to me that Anthropic didn’t just say they copied Mononoke and rebuilt it in 5 months. That is still noteworthy, even if it isn’t as grand. Surely they knew they would be called out?
It is always good to situate your work in the larger context.
We all stand on the shoulders of giants! There is nothing wrong with borrowing and adapting existing work to new contexts — that is the vast majority of what I do as an engineer. When you position your work as derivative, you are acknowledging those that came before you, as you hope to be acknowledged by those who come after you.
There is nothing without the team.
On a personal note, it’s been many years since I worked on Mononoke. There is a team that still carries the torch forward all these years later. Anthropic ripping the Bonsai data model off hit me hard, but spare a thought for the team working on it now: those who were most directly plagiarized. Imagine how they must feel about their work being
deliberately
copied wholesale and
intentionally
presented as someone else’s.
It’s been two days since I first posted about this on Bluesky and Linkedin, and I haven’t seen an update to the original post yet. This remains yet another shameful example of large AI companies appropriating the commons and presenting others’ work as their own. I don’t know what it will take to rebuild bridges from here, but my default assumption now is that Anthropic’s public engineering presentations are largely bad-faith ripoffs. That’s a shame.

Emma Roth
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.
President Donald Trump posted
a series of photos
on Truth Social showing off renovations to the White House — but
one of them appears
to be modified with AI. The picture, which compares an old White House column to a “restored” one, has several discrepancies and was flagged by Google’s AI detector as “made or edited with OpenAI.”
As
pointed out by users on Reddit
, the picture of the “restored” column has an uneven number of steps on both sides of the structure. The number of steps also doesn’t match up with the ones in the “before” photo. Additionally, the before and after photos appear nearly identical in angle and detail; the reflection in the windows is nearly the same, and the protective cardboard at the bottom of the column seems to be in the same spot as well. Not to mention that the “newly-painted” one looks unnaturally smooth.
Google’s SynthID detector flagged it as made or edited with OpenAI’s tools.
Screenshot: Emma Roth / The Verge
The Verge
can confirm that the photo posted to Truth Social is flagged as AI-generated when uploaded to
Google’s SynthID Detector
, which scans images, videos, and audio for an invisible watermark that indicates it was “created or edited” with AI.
Real pictures show people
painting the front of the White House in June
, so it’s possible the column actually did get a fresh coat of paint — the White House didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. The SynthID watermark wasn’t detected on other pictures Trump posted, which show the White House facade and heliport. Trump is no stranger to AI tools, though, as he often
posts AI-generated caricatures of himself
, while the White House has been known to
post racist AI memes
and at least one photo
deceptively edited
to make a protester appear distraught.

So I decided to buy a negative photo scanner and found that the Plustek 8200i was supported under Linux so I bought that. Only to discover that the chipset in the scanner had changed to one that wasn’t supported under Linux anymore. So I had some success making Linux configuration tools for some of my hardware using Claude code, like my [Dell Camera controller app](https://gitlab.com/cschalle/appfordellwebcam) so I thought, maybe Claude can help me get a working SANE driver. I basically got stuck and got nowhere for the longest time and even basically gave up on the project for a few Months.

Then I saw a [post on X from Tom Crider aka Glorious Eggroll](https://x.com/GloriousEggroll/status/2103816580966830314) talking about how he had managed to fix a mouse driver using AI tooling. He basically described how he set it up so that the AI agent had full control of a Windows instance to capture data needed to fix the driver. So I pasted his tweet into Claude and asked it to help me set up a windows virtual machine to do the same things Tom as doing for my scanner. I think the combination of having the ability to run scans under windows and capture the USB data while doing so worked wonders, probably combined with improvements to Claude code made a huge difference. Within a few hours I had my first ever working scan under Linux, sure with some quality issues, but 100% recognizable as the image in the negative. Some days later I had a near perfect driver, including support for Infrared scanning ready to go, only to discover that in the time between me giving up and then trying again someone had committed code to SANE to support the scanner already…..it happens sometimes. I also used Claude to write an application for doing negative scanning, which I named [Negative Vibes](https://github.com/cschalle/negative-vibes), thought that was a cute name.

Anyway, with the success of my scanner effort I thought, I wonder if I can use this to finally fix the last issues with MIPI camera support on my laptop. So I told claude to re-use the harness I had created and try to fix the MIPI camera on my laptop by updating the kernel driver and libcamera as needed. I started the job in the morning and by the end of the day I had [a much improved situation](https://cschalle.github.io/mipi-fixes-x1-aura/) with patches for both the kernel and libcamera ready.

So I thought that this might be worthwhile sharing with the world, and while anyone could start from scratch I did ask Claude to make the harness generic and document it to make the pathway for anyone else who wants to try this on their hardware a little easier. Writing a driver for undocumented hardware has always been tedious. You capture bus traffic, stare at hex dumps, and form hypotheses about what each register or control transfer does. You then test them one at a time, usually for weeks. None of it is conceptually hard, but it takes a lot of patience and skills.

That kind of work suits an AI model well. It can read thousands of lines of USB capture, notice that a sequence repeats with one byte changing, and propose what that byte means. It can write the test to confirm it, and it doesn’t get bored. The human still decides what to build and checks that it works on real hardware, but the slog shrinks a lot.

**[hw-harness](https://github.com/cschalle/hw-harness)**

Be aware that I did not use hw-harness in this form for my projects as this was basically bespoke code at that time, so this project is an attempt to make the harness more generic and shareable from the scripts I was using while doing the work. What hw-harness is meant to help your Claude or Codex session with:

1. Record a reference session. Run the vendor’s Windows driver in a KVM virtual machine, with the real device passed through to the guest.
 2. Capture from outside the VM. Record the traffic on the Linux host with usbmon. It sits below the passthrough layer, so the guest can’t see it.
 3. Repeat the same operation on Linux with your own driver, and capture that the same way.
 4. Diff the two traces. Both come from the same instrument, so they compare directly. The differences are your list of driver bugs.

For devices with no bus to tap, such as an internal MIPI camera, the harness uses Windows-side inspection instead. That means INF files, registry data, ACPI tables and device properties.

The approach should be fine in the sense it doesn’t rely on copying any code instead it observes what the hardware does and only extract configuration data from the Windows drivers, so every constant in the new driver traces back to something recorded.

So for those interested I have 3 short descriptions of the projects I did and what was needed.

**Project 1: [a SANE backend for the Plustek OpticFilm 8200i](https://htmlpreview.github.io/?https://github.com/cschalle/OpticFilm8200i-sane/blob/main/docs/comparison/drivers-comparison.html)**

Comparing the driver output of two drivers available.

The first project is a SANE backend for the newer Plustek OpticFilm 8200i. It uses the Genesys GL128 controller (USB 07b3:1825) and had no Linux support. The older model with the same name uses a GL845 and is already handled by SANE.

The backend supports:

*   Color, gray, infrared and color+infrared modes
*   Resolutions from 300 to 7200 dpi, at 8 or 16 bits per channel
*   Dust and scratch removal from the infrared channel
*   An exposure multiplier for dense negatives

It’s packaged as a Fedora RPM, built automatically on every push. I mostly tested it with my own Negative Vibes application as there are not that many options under Linux for negative scanning.

Upstream SANE’s genesys backend also gained support for this scanner in September 2026, so I compared the two. Both resolve the same fine detail at 3600 dpi. Mine is faster at full resolution (34.6 s against 54.4 s) and supports infrared dust removal. Upstream offers more resolution steps. The webpage has an interactive side-by-side comparison you can check out. These are single-unit, single-frame results, so treat them as one data point. [Check out the interactive page I made](https://htmlpreview.github.io/?https://github.com/cschalle/OpticFilm8200i-sane/blob/main/docs/comparison/drivers-comparison.html) showing the current state of the two drivers, hopefully the discoveries I made can be used by the SANE project to fix some smaller items in the upstream driver. Anyway, I put this project up more as a proof of concept due to that since I expect everyone including myself will use the upstream driver once it reaches parity with this one.

**Project 2: [Negative Vibes](https://github.com/cschalle/negative-vibes)**

Full scan of negative completed including infrared cleaning of image.

A driver alone isn’t much use if scanning negatives is still painful, so I built Negative Vibes. It’s a GNOME app, written in Rust, for scanning colour and black-and-white negatives and slides on any film-capable SANE scanner.

The scan is kept exactly as the scanner delivered it: 16-bit, linear, with the infrared plane. Everything else is a stack of non-destructive settings on top, so you can change the look and export again. It includes:

*   Density-space negative inversion with film base and dye-crosstalk correction
*   Roll-wide settings with per-frame overrides
*   Infrared and software dust removal
*   IT8 calibration through ArgyllCMS
*   Export to TIFF, JPEG, PNG and DNG, with ICC profiles and metadata

It ships as a Flatpak that includes the scanner backend. It’s tested on the 8200i so far. The goal is to support any film scanner SANE supports. For that, SANE needs a standard way to expose infrared channels, which it doesn’t have yet.

**Project 3: [Fixing the MIPI camera on my ThinkPad](https://cschalle.github.io/mipi-fixes-x1-aura/)**

Showing MIPI output before and after fixes. Colors are better than they look as I was sitting in a relatively dark room by the end of the session.

The camera in my Lenovo ThinkPad X1 Carbon Gen 14 (Aura Edition) uses a Sony IMX471 sensor behind an Intel IPU7. On Linux it produced dark images with heavy vignetting and a strong yellow-green cast. mipi-fixes-x1-aura collects the fixes. It’s only relevant to this laptop, which is why it isn’t one of the bigger packaged projects, but I have already submitted the kernel patches to Kate Hsuan and the libcamera patches is being reviewed by Wim Taymans for submission to Libcamera.

Kernel (IMX471 driver):

*   A crop-selection bug returned an error before storing the crop rectangle, so libcamera assumed the full pixel array.
*   The test-pattern register was declared with the wrong width.
*   The analogue gain cap was too low, which cost about 1.8 stops of sensitivity.

libcamera software ISP:

*   Lens shading correction was missing entirely, leaving the corners about 2.7 stops darker.
*   White-balance statistics were summed at the sensor’s native bit depth against an 8-bit black level. That skewed white balance, and the fix applies to any RAW10/RAW12 sensor.

In a controlled low-light test, frame brightness rose from 31.1 to 90.9. The red/green and blue/green ratios moved from 0.890 and 0.672 to 1.047 and 0.823, close to a USB webcam reference. Blue is still about 17% short in low light, which I put down to grey-world white balance. Fedora 44 RPMs are on the releases page.

What I learned

*   Reference captures are a big step. Having the AI compare a known-good trace against a failing one turns a vague “it doesn’t work” into a concrete list of differences. For example for the MIPI camera having a USB camera also connected so Claude could compare the two captures was critical.
*   The AI is good at the tedium. That covers decoding captures, writing probes and cross-checking constants. I still have to be the one holding the physical hardware.
*   Real hardware is the only judge. Every claim above was checked on the actual scanner or laptop.

If you have hardware with no Linux driver, try hw-harness. Thanks again to Glorious Eggroll for the inspiration.

**NOTE: I am not claiming that my scans or MIPI camera is perfect now, but the scanner gives me decent looking scans and the MIPI camera looks a lot better than before. So over time I am sure we be able to tweak and polish further, but I am happy that it allowed me to move the needle despite lacking the in-depth knowledge for this type of work.**

Sega is removing
Total War: Shogun 2 — Complete Edition
from storefronts following a disastrous launch where users complained about issues like bugs and upscaling that appears to have been done by AI.
Complete Edition
, a remaster of the 2011 strategy game, launched on Tuesday, and it bundled the main game and all of its DLC with promised upgrades including “improved visuals,” “1440p and 4K UI scaling,” and modernized controls. It has an “Overwhelmingly Negative” rating
on Steam
, where it has already been pulled, and
posts
on Reddit
showcase artwork that users believe AI messed up.
“We’re aware that
Total War: Shogun 2 – Complete Edition
has fallen short of both your expectations and our own standards,”
Sega and developer Creative Assembly wrote in a post
. “We’ve seen your feedback, comments, and reviews. We agree that the current experience is not where it needs to be.” The two companies say they will “reinstate the original game,” and existing owners will “still be able to access
” Complete Edition
.
Sega and Creative Assembly say that they are “working closely with our development partner to identify the causes of these problems, deliver improvements, and ensure Shogun 2 - Complete Edition meets the quality standards players expect from Total War.” A studio called Mataboo is also listed as a developer for the game on Steam, and Mataboo highlights its work on the game
on its website
.
